forces: Harp, flute, clarinet and string quartet
performers: Karen Grimsey, harp; Kara Santos, flute; Parker Gaims, clarinet; Sara Matayoshi and Foster Wang, violins; Tam Tran, viola; Clayton Vaughn, cello — United States Marine Band
intro: Ravel’s little harp concerto needs just seven players, yet its glissandos can fill a room. Karen Grimsey joins winds and strings from the United States Marine Band, then has the stage to herself in the long cadenza.

sections.label: Intro · Flute and clarinet open the door
sections.mNote: Strings join the wind duet before the harp enters

sections.label: A · The harp sings alone
sections.mNote: Allegro: a melody inside descending broken chords

sections.label: Dev · Harp and ensemble trade phrases
sections.mNote: Solo passages alternate with wind and string replies

sections.label: Cadenza · Arpeggios, chords and harp harmonics
sections.mNote: The other six players leave the harp alone

sections.label: Intro · Soft winds and muted strings
sections.mNote: The opening tempo returns around the harp

cues.title: The harp waits
cues.text: Flute and clarinet open in a soft duet. Violin, viola and cello join them; only then does the harp sweep upwards through their held notes. The second violin is still silent.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1906), p. 3, opening four bars. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IMSLP06186-Ravel_-_Introduction_et_Allegro,_score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A contest between harp makers
cues.text: Érard commissions Ravel in 1905 to show what its pedal harp can do. The rival firm Pleyel has already commissioned Debussy’s Danses for its chromatic harp. Ravel puts his instrument among flute, clarinet and four strings.
cues.evidence: Jane Vial Jaffe, programme note on the commissions from Pleyel and Érard: https://www.parlancechamberconcerts.org/individual-program-notes/maurice-ravel-%281875-1937%29/introduction-and-allegro.

cues.title: The harp takes the tune
cues.text: The Allegro leaves the harp almost alone. Its melody sits at the top of descending broken chords, marked le chant en dehors: the tune must stand out. Low harmonics ring beneath the quick notes.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 8, rehearsal 2: Allegro, le chant en dehors and harp harmonics beneath the melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The score at the shirt shop
cues.text: In 1905 Ravel rushes to finish the score before a holiday aboard Alfred and Misia Edwards’s yacht. He leaves the manuscript at a shirt shop, misses the boat, then has to persuade the music-loving shopkeeper to give it back. He catches up with the yacht at Soissons.
cues.evidence: The manuscript, chemisier and missed departure are recounted by Jane Vial Jaffe: https://www.parlancechamberconcerts.org/individual-program-notes/maurice-ravel-%281875-1937%29/introduction-and-allegro.

cues.title: Six players fall silent
cues.text: The harp has a cadenza. Arpeggios climb from the bass, slow chords interrupt them, and glissandos lead into delicate harmonics. Karen Grimsey supplies the melody, bass and ringing after-sound on her own.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 26–27: Cadenza, rubato, Lent, Très lent, glissandos and harmonics.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The winds return softly
cues.text: Flute and clarinet return at ppp, with muted strings around the harp. The cello plucks its notes. Ravel restores the introduction’s tempo so quietly that the cadenza seems to have acquired companions.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 27, rehearsal 18: 1° Tempo, ppp winds, muted strings and pizzicato cello.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A clarinet above the harp
cues.text: The harp’s flowing Allegro figures return, but the clarinet now carries the tune above them. The other players wait. Plucked notes tumble underneath a melody that can hold its breath.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 29, rehearsal 20: solo clarinet above harp figuration; flute and strings rest.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A last sweep of strings
cues.text: The harp sweeps through its final glissandos while the string quartet switches to pizzicato. Flute and clarinet give short, bright answers. All seven players share the last G♭-major chord.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 39: final harp glissandos, pizzicato strings, wind attacks and G♭-major close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The ensemble leaves the harp singing
transitions.from: Intro · Flute and clarinet open the door
transitions.how: At Allegro, winds and strings release their held notes while the harp begins its descending broken chords. Ravel marks the tune le chant en dehors. Harmonics sustain the bass beneath it; the other six instruments fall silent.

transitions.title: The harp inherits the bass
transitions.from: Dev · Harp and ensemble trade phrases
transitions.to: Cadenza · Arpeggios, chords and harp harmonics
transitions.how: The ensemble holds a chord while the harp starts low arpeggios, marked Cadenza and rubato. As the winds and strings release, the arpeggios climb through the space they leave. Slower chords and harmonics follow under Lent and Très lent.

transitions.title: Muted strings around the harp
transitions.from: Cadenza · Arpeggios, chords and harp harmonics
transitions.to: Intro · Soft winds and muted strings
transitions.how: The harp’s harmonics lead into 1° Tempo. Flute and clarinet return at ppp, the bowed strings put on mutes, and the cello plucks a quiet bass. The harp continues beneath the opening’s sustained phrases.

transitions.title: The clarinet sings the harp’s tune
transitions.from: Intro · Soft winds and muted strings
transitions.how: The harp resumes its Allegro arpeggios as the ensemble releases its chord. At rehearsal 20 the clarinet enters quietly with the melody, above the harp’s flowing notes and low harmonics. Flute and strings remain silent for this duet.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 28–29, Allegro and rehearsal 20.

source.title: Ravel, Introduction et Allegro — original seven-player full score, Durand, 1906
source.locator: Opening and rehearsals 2, 4, 18 and 20; printed pp. 3, 8, 11, 26–30 and 39. One player takes each of the seven parts.

timeline.note: Flute and clarinet begin alone, in a soft duet.
First violin, viola and cello join the winds before the harp sweeps upwards. Second violin waits.
All seven players join the introduction’s closing phrases before the harp’s solo Allegro.
The harp begins the Allegro with a melody inside descending broken chords. The ensemble’s held chord releases.
Flute sings above the harp’s arpeggios and harmonics. Violins move in quick notes; the cello plucks its bass.
The harp takes the cadenza alone, climbing through arpeggios before slower chords and harmonics.
Flute and clarinet return softly, with muted strings and harp. The cello plucks its notes.
The harp’s Allegro figures return, then the clarinet enters with the melody above them.
Flute and strings rejoin the clarinet and harp. The wind phrases climb over the harp’s continuing arpeggios.

facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
